name: Iowa Statue of Liberty
title: Iowa's Boy Scout Statue of Liberty
description: An 8-foot-4-inch sheet-copper Statue of Liberty replica, given to Iowa in 1950, stands on the State Capitol grounds in Des Moines.
subtitle: Boy Scout replica on the Capitol grounds
lede: A sheet-copper Statue of Liberty, 8 feet 4 inches tall, stands on the Iowa State Capitol grounds. The Tall Corn Council of the Boy Scouts gave it to the state in 1950.

paragraphs: The Iowa Legislature's Capitol tour text says the Tall Corn Council of the Boy Scouts of America, now the Mid-Iowa Council, donated this replica to the State of Iowa in 1950 as part of its annual service project. The statue stands 8 feet 4 inches tall and is made of 47 pieces of sheet copper.

That same account credits the idea to Jack Whitaker, a Kansas City businessman active in the Boy Scouts. After seeing a chicken-wire and concrete Statue of Liberty in Spirit Lake, Iowa, he paid to have a mold made. Scout troops then bought replicas and presented them to cities and towns across the country.

A historical marker beside the Des Moines figure quotes the Boy Scouts' 40th Anniversary Crusade to Strengthen the Arm of Liberty and dates the dedication to 1950. The Historical Marker Database places the marker on 12th Street south of Grand Avenue, near the northeast corner of the Capitol grounds in the East Village.

paragraphs: The City of Elk Horn's Kimballton directory says that in 1974 the Progressive Danes of Kimballton bought a mermaid sculpted by two college students in Modesto, California. It is a replica of the Little Mermaid in Copenhagen harbor and honors Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale. After the figure deteriorated, it was recast in bronze. In 2008 the statue and the Hans Christian Andersen Park were rededicated during Kimballton's quasquicentennial.

Roadside America says a fiberglass Little Mermaid was installed in town in 1978, was moved indoors each winter, and was recast in bronze by 2008. It says the figure was rededicated, with a new fountain and landscaping, at the town's 125th anniversary celebration in June 2008. The two accounts agree on the 2008 bronze recasting; they do not agree on whether the first version was cold-cast bronze in 1974 or fiberglass in 1978.

Troy Muller, art director of the New Century Art Guild in Kimballton, designed eight sculptures based on Andersen stories for the garden. Marne and Elk Horn Telephone Company offers a call-in menu at 712-773-4267 so visitors can hear a three-minute synopsis of each fairy tale. The park also includes the Audubon County Freedom Rock. Roadside America places Mermaid Park at 310 N. Main St., on the east side of the street just south of Highway 44, next to a half-sized replica windmill.

name: The Black Angel
title: The Black Angel at Oakland Cemetery
description: An 8.5-foot bronze angel at Oakland Cemetery turned black from oxidation after Teresa Feldevert commissioned it.
subtitle: Feldevert monument in Oakland Cemetery
lede: Oakland Cemetery's 8.5-foot Black Angel is a bronze monument for the Feldevert family. The City of Iowa City says the dark color is oxidation, and it asks visitors not to touch the monuments.
paragraphs: The City of Iowa City says Oakland Cemetery, at 1000 Brown Street, holds an 8.5-foot monument called the Black Angel, erected for the Feldevert family in 1912. Teresa Dolezal Feldevert was born in 1836 in Strmilov, Bohemia. Her son Eddie Dolezal died of meningitis in 1891 at age 18 and was buried in the cemetery. After her husband Nicholas Feldevert died in 1911, she returned to Iowa City and commissioned Bohemian artist Mario Korbel, then in Chicago, to design a $5,000 bronze monument. The angel arrived on a flatcar on November 21, 1912.

The city says oral history places the installation in 1912, while other publications say it sat in a barn and was not erected until 1918 after Teresa lost a court case over the $5,000 price and the missing tree-stump detail. Eddie's tree-stump marker was later moved beside the angel. His remains and Nicholas's ashes were placed in repositories under it. Teresa died of cancer on November 18, 1924, and her ashes were buried there too.

The city says the bronze is black because the metal oxidized in the weather, and that the color change from a golden bronze cast fed myths that outlasted the documented history. Cemetery rules say to look and enjoy but not touch the monuments, and rubbings are not allowed. The grounds are open daily from 7:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m.

paragraphs: The Southern Indiana Business Report says Otis, a 25-foot sasquatch at French Lick Cabins at Patoka Lake, was completed in April 2023 by the Bear Hollow carving team. Owners Jason and Cindy Emmons said visitors began showing up in school buses, motorcycle groups, and Jeeps. Otis later appeared on the cover of Indiana's official spring/summer 2024 travel magazine, seated on a fishing dock with a pole.

Nine carvers, including Jason Emmons and his son Ethan, built Otis on site in about four days after about six months of planning. The frame is treated lumber from Paoli Bender Lumber. Twelve bundles of poplar sawmill slabs became the fur, and solid white pine logs became the face and feet. The report says the dock bows under his weight and a red and white bobber hangs from the pole.

paragraphs: An Indiana State Museum account says that in June 1816, while the capitol was unfinished, 43 delegates left an overheated log cabin and met under the elm. The tree spread more than 130 feet across and stood 50 feet tall. It became known as the Constitution Elm.

paragraphs: The City of Wichita says the Keeper stands at the confluence of the Big and Little Arkansas rivers with hands raised in supplication to the Great Spirit. Blackbear Bosin donated it to the citizens of Wichita in 1974. It was dedicated May 18, 1974, with Senator Bob Dole present, for the U.S. Bicentennial. The 44-foot Cor-Ten steel figure now stands on a 30-foot rock promontory. An eight-year, $20 million river project was completed in May 2007, and the renovated Keeper was dedicated on May 18, 2007.

Visit Wichita calls it a five-ton, 44-foot steel sculpture and says five fire drums illuminate it. The city says the Ring of Fire burns nightly for 15 minutes and is run by hand. It is not lit in high wind, rain, or other bad weather, if the river is too high, or if a person or goose is too close to the burners. Daylight saving time hours are 9:00 to 9:15 p.m.; standard time is 7:00 to 7:15 p.m. Visit Wichita says the 15 minutes symbolize the sacred hoop of earth, air, water, and fire.

Both the city and Visit Wichita say the plaza is free and open from 5 a.m. to midnight. Two cable-stay bridges inspired by a bow and arrow cross the rivers. During the day, visitors can enter the plaza from the Mid-America All-Indian Museum, which charges admission. City ordinance 11.16.085 bans skateboarding on the plaza and bridges. As of the city page, trail and parking-lot work near the Keeper was expected to last until November 2026, with a temporary path for pedestrians.

description: Enid Yandell's bronze Daniel Boone, unveiled June 15, 1906, stands at the Eastern Parkway entrance to Cherokee Park.
subtitle: Enid Yandell's bronze at Cherokee Park
lede: Louisville's Daniel Boone Monument is Enid Yandell's bronze pioneer, unveiled on June 15, 1906, at the Eastern Parkway entrance to Cherokee Park. It is not a stone cairn.

paragraphs: Olmsted Parks Conservancy says Enid Yandell first made the Daniel Boone figure for the Kentucky Building at the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago, commissioned by what is now the Filson Historical Society. She used Boone's hunting shirt, rifle, tomahawk, knife, and powder horn while shaping the likeness. Businessman C.C. Bickel later paid to have it cast in bronze and installed at the Eastern Parkway entrance of Cherokee Park.

Louisville Metro's public-art record dates the bronze-and-limestone statue to 1906 and says Charles C. Bickel, a local architect, asked Yandell for the permanent bronze. The unveiling on June 15, 1906, included a Boone family reception and a staged fort attack. The record says the statue was moved from a shallow alcove in Cherokee Park, where Boone was meant to look as if he were coming out of the woods, to a more visible spot in the Cherokee Triangle off Eastern Parkway.

A Kentucky Historical Society marker for Yandell, number 2133, erected in 2004, lists two noted Louisville works: the Daniel Boone Monument and Hogan's Fountain. That marker stands at Cherokee Road and Cherokee Park Road, which is a marker site rather than a measured pin for the statue itself.

name: Jefferson Monument (Louisville, Kentucky)
title: Jefferson Monument at Metro Hall
description: Moses Ezekiel's bronze Thomas Jefferson, given by the Bernheim brothers in 1901, stands on a Liberty Bell outside Metro Hall.
subtitle: Ezekiel's bronze outside Metro Hall
lede: Moses Jacob Ezekiel's Thomas Jefferson stands outside Louisville Metro Hall on a bronze Liberty Bell. The Bernheim brothers gave the monument to the city in November 1901.
paragraphs: Wikipedia, drawing on the 1902 Monumental News, says Moses Jacob Ezekiel's Jefferson Monument stands outside Louisville Metro Hall. The Bernheim brothers presented it to Louisville in November 1901. The bronze figure is 9 feet high and shows Jefferson at age 33 presenting the Declaration of Independence. He stands on a bronze Liberty Bell 9 feet high and nearly 10 feet in diameter. Four figures on the bell represent Liberty, Equality, Justice, and the Brotherhood of Man. The lower part is dark Quincy granite. The whole monument is 25 feet high. Clarke & Loomis of Louisville were the constructing architects, the bronze was cast in Berlin, and Ezekiel made the models in his Rome studio.

Louisville Metro's public-art record dates the bronze to 1901 and says the Bernheim brothers approached Ezekiel in 1899. It places the work on the front lawn of the former Jefferson County Courthouse at 527 West Jefferson Street, now Louisville Metro Hall. It identifies the four winged figures as Liberty, Justice, Religious Freedom, and Equality, also called the Brotherhood of Man or Human Freedom. A catalog image is captioned as Justice before the theft of her scales. The record also points to a Courier-Journal unveiling story dated November 10, 1901. A smaller replica was placed at the University of Virginia in 1910.
